newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: New man, new approach seen at SAfrica central bank.
newsitem.headline: New man, new approach seen at SAfrica central bank.

text.p: The South African Reserve Bank's appointment of James Cross as a deputy governor signals the central bank's determination to break with the turbulence of 1996, foreign exchange commentators said on Tuesday.
Analysts have lauded the move, pointing to Cross' experience in the foreign exchange markets as pivotal to the central bank's intentions to reduce volatililty in South African markets.
He was appointed as one of the bank's three deputy governors late last year and took up his appointment this month.
Bank Governor Chris Stals announced on Monday night that he had placed Cross in charge of the bank's exchange control, international banking and money and capital market departments.

"The Reserve Bank team has been boosted by the fact the James Cross is now back as deputy governor of the Reserve Bank," said one head of Treasury who asked not to be named. "He has tremendous experience of managing foreign exchange volatility."

Dave Sadler, chief dealer in foreign exchange at First National Bank, said: "He is a man who has been brought up within the markets, so his understanding of foreign exchange and what needs to be done is going to be of benefit."

Cross worked in the commercial banking sector from 1968 before focussing on international treasury management from 1978 onwards. Between 1985 and 1986, he was head of trading at Union Bank of Switzerland in London before returning to South Africa later in 1986.
He served as general manager of the Reserve Bank from 1987 to July 1995, before joining a cosultancy in London for 18 months.
Sadler said that while Cross' appointment was positive for the foreign exchange market, it had also raised hopes for greater clarity on exchange controls.
"I think that people will be looking for a lot more positive things from Cross on exchange controls," Sadler said, adding that the market would look to Cross for a clearer timeframe on their removal.
Cross is believed to have the liberalisation of exchange controls at the top of his agenda.

Perceptions that Cross favours a more stable rand has also prompted market speculation that the Reserve Bank could buy dollars as the currency strengthens -- a move that would also bolster the paltry state of its reserves.
"The market knows that James Cross is in for a more stable currency. The talk is that the Bank might be looking to buy dollars below 4.58 in order to reduce volatility in the market," a trader said.
Cross said that while the central bank favoured a more stable currency, it had to reflect market realities.
"It would be nice to see a more stable rand but at the same time it has got to reflect what is going on and market perceptions," Cross told Reuters.
"We would like confidence in our currency to increase but there is no targetting," he added.
Cross said that the rand's 13 cent strengthening on the dollar since the beginning of the year apppeared to stem from a shift in market perceptions.

"What a volatile currency does is make everybody uncertain. That includes your corporate sector...they don't know where to turn or what to do. That is when you do not like the situation and that is when I think the central bank can be useful.
"But the underlying market trends and fundamentals must take their course," Cross said.
